extracted.intended_audience: congressional staff, administrative law practitioners, agency rulewriters, and lawyers interested in federal rulemaking and judicial review
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes procedural and substantive legal standards that govern how federal agencies promulgate, amend, or repeal rules (including notice-and-comment, formal, hybrid, direct final, negotiated rulemaking) and how courts review those actions under the APA and related doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of rule and rulemaking (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'rule' is any 'agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy or describing the organization, procedure, or practice requirements of an agency.' Rulemaking is the 'agency process for formulating, amending, or repealing a rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules issued in compliance with legal requirements and within delegated authority have the force and effect of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal rulemaking (5 U.S.C. § 553) — notice requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When promulgating legislative rules, agencies must provide adequate notice of a proposed rule, generally via publication of a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice must include (1) the time, place, and nature of public rulemaking proceedings; (2) reference to the legal authority under which the rule is proposed; and (3) either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal rulemaking — meaningful opportunity to comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must provide interested persons a meaningful opportunity to comment by submitting written 'data, views, or arguments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no set minimum comment period; courts evaluate adequacy of opportunity by considering multiple factors (length of period is only one). Comments may result in a large rulemaking record; agencies must consider 'relevant matter presented.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rule — concise general statement of basis and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: After the comment period, the APA directs the agency to consider relevant matter presented and incorporate into the adopted rule a 'concise general statement' of the 'basis and purpose' of the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should enable the public to obtain a general idea of the purpose of, and a statement of the basic justification for, the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to comments — obligation to address 'significant' comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency is not required to respond to every comment received; it is obligated only to respond to what courts have characterized as 'significant' comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must respond sufficiently to permit meaningful judicial review of whether the agency considered important issues raised during comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and 30-day delayed effective date requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule and the general statement must be published in the Federal Register not less than 30 days before the rule's effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are exceptions (see separate entries). Publication and, for many non-legislative rules, public availability requirements still apply even if notice-and-comment exemption applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal rulemaking requirements (§ 556, § 557) — 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing'
rubrics_metrics.description: When statutes require rulemaking 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing,' agencies must follow formal rulemaking with trial-like procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal proceedings require opportunity to present oral or documentary evidence, cross-examination, presiding official or ALJ with power to administer oaths and issue subpoenas, prohibition on ex parte communications, agency bears burden of proof, and rules must be supported by 'substantial evidence' on the whole record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid rulemaking — added procedural requirements by statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may direct agencies to follow specific procedural requirements in addition to § 553, creating hybrid rulemaking that is more flexible than formal rulemaking but allows more public participation than informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hybrid statutes may require hearings, oral testimony, opportunities for cross examination or questioning; they apply only when Congress expressly directs them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-final rulemaking procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may publish a proposed rule as 'direct final' with language that the rule will become effective on a date unless an adverse comment is received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an adverse comment is received, the proposed rule is withdrawn and reissued under normal notice-and-comment. Justifications for direct-final procedures include the 'unnecessary' portion of the APA 'good cause' exception and efficiency for noncontroversial rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated rulemaking procedures (Negotiated Rulemaking Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may establish a negotiated rulemaking committee to negotiate and develop a proposed rule if in the public interest; committees must comply with FACA and related notice requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee generally limited to 25 members with at least one agency representative; public has opportunity to comment on committee creation and membership; committee reports are not binding and any proposed rule must still be finalized through ordinary notice-and-comment procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholly exempt categories from § 553
rubrics_metrics.description: APA exempts rules relating to (1) a military or foreign affairs function; (2) a matter relating to agency management or personnel; or (3) a matter relating to public property, loans, grants, benefits, or contracts from procedural requirements of § 553.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exempt rules still have the force and effect of law. The 'property' exception is limited (e.g., distribution of property). The management exception only applies where the rule would not affect parties outside the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-legislative rules exemption (interpretive rules, policy statements, procedure/practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive rules, general statements of policy, and rules of agency organization, procedure, or practice are exempt from notice-and-comment requirements and typically do not carry the force of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are allowed so agencies can provide timely guidance; interpretive rules 'only remind affected parties of existing duties'; general statements of policy announce tentative intentions. However, if a purported 'procedure' substantially affects external rights or decisions, notice-and-comment may be required. Non-legislative rules must still satisfy publication and public availability provisions and may be effective immediately upon publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination whether action is legislative or non-legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must decide whether an action interprets existing law or results in a substantive change; the characterization affects required procedures and judicial deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency cannot go beyond the text of a statute and exercise delegated powers without providing adequate notice-and-comment; courts look at whether the action creates new rights/duties or simply explains existing law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause exception to notice-and-comment (§ 553(b)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may dispense with notice-and-comment when they find the use of traditional procedures is 'impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must give supporting reasons; courts narrowly construe and reluctantly countenance good cause. The inquiry is fact-specific and considers immediacy, consequences of inaction, and whether advance notice would defeat the regulatory objective. 'Bald assertions' that comments would be useless do not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim final rules and post-promulgation comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies sometimes issue interim final rules (final rules effective immediately) while reserving the right to modify the rule through a post-promulgation comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim final rules require assertion of valid good cause; Congress has authorized interim final rules for specific programs; ACUS recommended post-promulgation comments where impracticable or contrary-to-public-interest prongs are invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to the 30-day delayed effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain rules are exempt from the APA's 30-day waiting period (e.g., interpretive rules, policy statements, rules for which agency finds 'good cause,' and 'a substantive rule which grants or recognizes an exemption or relieves a restriction').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeals that relieve a restriction may be exempt from the delayed effective date; rules qualifying for these exceptions may be effective upon publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for amending or repealing rules — same APA requirements generally apply
rubrics_metrics.description: To amend or repeal an existing legislative rule, an agency generally must comply with the same notice-and-comment procedures that governed the original promulgation of the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If statute establishing the rule required alternative procedures, those procedures may apply to amendment/repeal as well. Non-legislative pronouncements not subject to notice-and-comment may be altered immediately without public participation, but Perez v. Mortgage Bankers makes clear agencies must use same procedures when they amend or repeal a rule as when they issued it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delaying implementation of final rules — limits and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies generally may not simply suspend the effectiveness of an existing rule, but may implement temporary delays of new final rules that have been published but not yet taken effect (often used during presidential transitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an agency may postpone effective dates without notice-and-comment is unsettled; some courts view such delays as substantive amendments requiring notice-and-comment. Courts more readily permit delays when a rule is subject to a pending legal challenge. APA §705 permits postponement 'when an agency finds that justice so requires.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Orders — OIRA review and cost-benefit requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Orders (beginning with Reagan) require OIRA (in OMB) to review 'significant' regulatory actions at proposed and final stages; they direct agencies to perform cost-benefit analyses and to adopt regulations only upon a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA review precludes issuing a rule while review is pending 'except to the extent required by law.' Independent agencies may voluntarily comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13771 — regulatory offset requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 13771 directed agencies to offset the costs of new rules in FY2017 by repealing existing rules so that the total incremental cost of new regulations would be no greater than zero, with several specified exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order applies only to executive branch agencies, to 'significant' regulatory actions generally defined as >$100 million economic impact, and contains exemptions for military/national security, agency organization rules, and rules required by law or imminent statutory/judicial deadlines. Agencies still must comply with APA when implementing offsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of judicial review under the APA and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong presumption that Congress intends judicial review of administrative action; APA makes final agency action subject to judicial review unless other statutes preclude it or action is committed to agency discretion by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine statutory language and legislative and judicial history to determine whether review is precluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §706 grounds for setting aside agency action (A–F)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing court shall hold unlawful and set aside agency action found to be: (A) arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law; (B) contrary to constitutional right, power, privilege, or immunity; (C) in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority, or limitations, or short of statutory right; (D) without observance of procedure required by law; (E) unsupported by substantial evidence in cases subject to §§556–557; or (F) unwarranted by the facts to the extent facts are subject to trial de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type of review may differ (substantial evidence for formal on-the-record proceedings; arbitrary and capricious for informal rulemakings), but the line between standards has in practice sometimes converged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: 'substantial evidence' review vs 'arbitrary and capricious' review
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases subject to §§556–557 (formal, on-the-record) are reviewed for 'substantial evidence'; other agency actions are subject to 'arbitrary and capricious' review, though commentators note convergence in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some statutes may require substantial evidence review for otherwise informal rulemaking; courts may treat standards similarly in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary and capricious standard — required elements (State Farm)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court should not substitute its judgment for the agency; it should invalidate agency determinations that fail to 'examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for [the] action including a 'rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must consider relevant factors, avoid clear errors of judgment, not rely on factors Congress did not intend, not entirely fail to consider an important aspect of the problem, not offer an explanation counter to evidence, and not make implausible choices that cannot be ascribed to expertise. This is often described as 'hard look' review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned decisionmaking requirement and evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency must demonstrate that it engaged in reasoned decisionmaking by providing an adequate explanation and the essential facts upon which the decision was based, supported by actual evidence beyond conclusory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions produced by illogical or inconsistent reasoning, failure to consider important policy effects or problem aspects, or failure to consider less restrictive alternatives will fail review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review of agency change or repeal — reasoned analysis for change
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency changes position, it must provide a 'reasoned analysis for the change' though not a more stringent standard simply because it alters prior policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Fox Television: (1) agency must 'display awareness' it is changing position; (2) need not show new policy is better than old one—only that there are 'good reasons' and it's permissible under the statute; (3) more detailed justification may be required when the new policy rests on factual findings that contradict prior findings or where prior policy engendered 'serious reliance interests.' Encino Motorcars emphasizes that decades of industry reliance may require more reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to agency statutory interpretations (Chevron/Mead variety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts grant varying levels of deference to agency interpretations of statutes when examining whether agency action is within delegated authority; the amount of deference varies with circumstances and doctrine such as Chevron and Mead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An administrative agency's power to regulate must be grounded in valid congressional authority; amount of deference depends on whether statute is ambiguous, whether agency interpretation is reasonable, and related jurisprudential factors (see CRS Report R43203 for details).
